Is just an old, ingrained trope. Something similar is from older cinema, where when a character would be introduced, the screen would freeze and their name would appear. I don't think it's a matter of telling and not showing, especially given how your example includes them showing. It exists in fighting games too. When a character performs a special move, you know it's that move, you don't have to take their word for it. It's not meant to handhold the viewer and explain what it is; I think it's just a dramatic element of introduction that audiences may differ on.

Your example of fighting games is actually a very prime example; there are special attack techniques that the characters often name out so that the players are aware they are special and different, and not just a simple combo move.

Then why isn't it done for every special move? Some characters rarely do it, for example. One character cries out the name of their fireball or dragon punch, but there are on-screen visual indicators that these aren't just punches; they're flaming and look special. Meanwhile, another character's specials are still just punches, and they don't have any accompanying name telegraphing. Surely if the naming of moves had to do with balance and hand-holding, everyone would do it to make it fair, especially the character whose normals and specials are both punches with decidedly less fire radiating off of them.

Instead, the ones getting audibly introduced are the ones that also have visual recognition - the recognizable moves that a seasoned player could identify long before the character starts talking about it - because the introduction is for drama, not gameplay.

Anyone playing can tell that a special move, even before the character yells, is not just a normal punch. The naming has nothing to do with it; the character is throwing a powerful energy projectile. But at the same time, another character is never shouting out the names of his moves, which, whether normal or special, are still just ordinary punches.

Yes, the shout does help player response in a way, but I highly doubt that was intentional; it just became a way to time the move because it was happening.

The moves that get audible names are often the most flashy of the special moves, which leads me to think it is entirely similar to how it's used in films or television shows.

but instead created a precedent for other games to learn from. Powerful moves in most modern games have some sort of flashy way to signify what is happening, and the easiest way to do that is to have a character tell you.

As someone else mentioned, even more fighting games don't do this.

It also makes games more accessible because even a new player understands that the enemy isn't going to shout out weak and ordinary move names, so they know to block.

Many characters, even in a popular fighting game series, don't do it. None of a certain character's special punches have a visual or audible cue to set them apart from normal punches.

I agree that the naming of the move does help to some degree, but it's an unintended side effect.

However, the first animated series that did it, their reasoning was as I said.

That said, I think we're just saying the same thing in different ways. I don't see it as handholding; I see it as a different culture's way of heightening the drama for a specific situation. It's a very eastern cliché that is rooted in traditions that don't really exist on the other side of the world. You don't need to hear a narrative explanation to know why a character's fireball attack is any stronger than their punch, or even any other fireball - there's all kinds of pageantry around it that does it other than simply giving it a name. Giving it the name isn't skipping the storytelling to tell you that it's now suddenly stronger; giving the name/sounds to go with it makes it stronger. Eastern cinema, and a lot of the culture, just really likes verbosity and titling things that don't really need an introduction - which is what the original poster is referencing in the first place.

The audience will realize it's stronger without the quirk. Most animated series, especially older ones, use a lot of recycled footage of long start-ups and "powering up" for strong moves. It has nothing to do with shouting its name - even if that may often be a part of it.
